Provenance: Augustus the Strong (1670-1733), Elector of Saxony and King of Poland (engraved Dresden inventory mark on the base of the dish reading N:266), recorded 1779 (Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden Palace Inventory 1779 Entry)
Jeremy Mason, London

Augustus the Strong (Augustus II), Elector of Saxony and King of Poland (1670-1733) was an avid art collector. He amassed an extensive collection of porcelain which was housed in the 'Japanese Palace' in Dresden.

The inventory record for this piece is dated 1779 and reads 'Nine copper dishes of varying size, their ground lacquered in white and painted with flowers and butterflies in polychrome, the largest 2½ inches deep and 17½ inches in diam., the smallest 1½ inches deep and 11 inches in diam., many defective, No. 266.'

Three companion dishes from the original set to which the present lot belongs remain in the Dresden Porcelain Collection (inv.no.PO 973, 974 and 975).

The last of these is published in R.Friedrich, Die Porzellansammlung Augusts des Starken. Porzellankunst aus China - Die Rosa Familie, München, 1993.

Jeremy Mason is a noted bibliophile and dealer in Chinese and Japanese art who started his career at Christie's in the late 1960s, particularly known for his collection of Oscar Wilde books and ephemera, sold by Bonhams London in February 2026. His Chinese art collection was housed in his 18th century townhouse, Hoyle's House, London, some pieces for the last 50 years.

This charming rendering illustrates a scene from Oliver Goldsmith's second play, She Stoops to Conquer, which debuted at the Covent Garden Theatre on 15th March 1773. The narrative was based on an embarrassing anecdote from Goldsmith's own student days in Ireland, when he was tricked into believing the local squire's house was an inn and brashly ordered dinner and a night's lodging. In the play, Tony Lumpkin, represented by the actor John Quick (1748-1831), a youth from the wealthy Hardcastle family, dupes two travellers named Marlow and Hastings into believing his home to be a public house. The title She Stoops to Conquer refers to Tony's sister Kate Hardcastle represented here by the actor Jane Green (née Hippisley) (1719-1791), who, as part of the scheme, pretends to be the barmaid in order to win the hero Marlow, who has a fear of upper-class ladies. He is seen beside Mr Hardcastle, played by Edward Shuter (1728?-1776), pleading with him not to be angry at the news that Tony was complicit in his joke.

The reverse glass painting appears to be taken from a mezzotint engraving published in 1776. This in turn was taken from an original painting was sold by Christie's New York, 28 January 2009, lot 285.

A paper note affixed to reverse of the painting states:

History of General Peng Yueh Ling, hung on staircase, brought at Hong Kong by Mr Sanford Graves at Hong Kong from his granddaughter, a refugee from Peking, wife of a schoolmaster, a sweet little Chinese lady looked about 17 (mother of 5 children)

The Portrait is General Peng Yueh Ling, one of the distinguished Generals of Chin Dynasty who suppressed Tai-Ping Rebellion during the beginning of 19th Century. He was native of Hupei, a military genius, founded new military training system in China.

History of portrait... purchased by me in Hong Kong May 1939 from a refugee from Peking

Peng Yulin (1817-1890) is known as both an artist and pre-eminent military leader. He fell in love with the adopted daughter of his maternal grandmother, Meigu (plum blossom), but the match was rejected, she married another man, and died. Peng vowed to complete 10,000 paintings of plum blossom, to commemorate the namesake of his lost love.

This he did alongside a stellar military career. He rose to become Minister of War after a legendary military career in which he helped defeat the Taiping Army through his actions in the battles of Yuezhou and Tianjiazhen. A painting of plum blossom by the artist was sold by Bonhams London, 16 May 2023, lot 368.

清 一八二零至一八八零年 仕女鼻烟壺

Provenance: A private collection, London
Robert Hall, London
A private collection, Edinburgh, acquired from the above 12th December 2013 (invoice)

Published and Illustrated: The Heriot Collection of Chinese Snuff Bottles, Volume I, Edinburgh, 2020, p.8, fig.78

Small figurative carvings known as 'medicine ladies' or 'doctor's models' are most commonly preserved as ivory carvings, based on the notion that when a doctor visited a woman she would reach through the curtains of her bed and touch the ivory figure to indicate the spot causing her trouble. They have been said to derive from Sino-Spanish ivory figures of the infant Jesus that would have been seen by Chinese craftsmen during the Ming dynasty.

This snuff bottle group is known, see for example, M.Hughes, The Blair Bequest, Chinese Snuff Bottles from the Princeton University Museum, Hong Kong, 2002, nos.297-299. The present example is apparently unique, however, in depicting the lady in a state of significant physical ailment with lumps to her neck and chest, and swollen drooling lips.

Provenance: Dr Walter Rieder (1890-1986)

Dr Walter Rieder (1890-1986) served in the Swiss East Asia Mission (SOAM) in Qingdao, Shandong Province, between October 1930 and December 1951. The mission specialised in educational, literary and philanthropic work and Dr Rieder was in fact, not a theologian or missionary, but a teacher of mathematics, physics and science to high school students attached to the SOAM. His guiding principles were 'Creating understanding between different cultures' and 'Building bridges between East and West'. While in Qingdao, Dr Rieder collected a wide variety of Chinese art. The objects in the collection thus offer a unique window into the type of antiques that were on the market in Qingdao in the second quarter of the 20th century. As well as demonstrating his passion for Chinese art, his collection also reveals the personal friendships Dr Rieder forged with local artists, some of whom he knew from his teaching activities. Dr Rieder had a scholarly approach to studying his collection. Alongside many of his objects, meticulous notes can sometimes be found detailing his art historical commentaries. The collection was hence Dr Rieder's gateway to the history and culture of China. Objects from the collection were exhibited at the Kunsthaus in Interlaken, Switzerland in 2006 and 2018.

The objects in the collection thus offer a unique window into the type of antiques that were on the market in Qingdao in the second quarter of the 20th century. As well as demonstrating his passion for Chinese art, his collection also reveals the personal friendships Dr Rieder forged with local artists, some of whom he knew from his teaching activities. Dr Rieder had a scholarly approach to studying his collection. Alongside many of his objects, meticulous notes can sometimes be found detailing his art historical commentaries. The collection was hence Dr Rieder's gateway to the history and culture of China. Objects from the collection were exhibited at the Kunsthaus in Interlaken, Switzerland in 2006 and 2018.

Her art often focused on subjects such as the "Four Noble Ones" (Sikunshi—orchids, bamboo, plum blossoms, and chrysanthemums), a motif deeply rooted in literati culture that symbolised elegance and refined virtue.

Many female artists at that time were not properly documented and were therefore forgotten by history. But Shokin made a name for herself through her artistic and literary talents, by 1853, she was famous for her paintings and received numerous commissions.

Thence by descent

Exhibited: On long-term loan to West Park Museum, Macclesfield, circa 1939-1976

Both brothers were extensive travellers and explorers, Sir Philip having been on Shackleton's 1907-1909 Nimrod expedition to the Antarctic and who later travelled through both the Middle and Far East. His brother Courtney, who went with him to the Arctic in 1912 and later became game warden of the Sudan in the 1920s, then went on to travel extensively in China, Japan and Tibet in the 1930s, bringing back the first giant panda from Tibet to the UK.

Many of the artefacts collected on these travels were put on loan at the West Park Museum, which had been built by the Brocklehurst family for safe keeping during the war, and when he was killed in 1942 fighting with the Chindits in Burma, his brother Philip inherited the contents of the museum where they remained until after his death in 1975.

Provenance: Harry Geoffrey Beasley (1881-1939), Topsham (label - no.4)

Harry Geoffrey Beasley was a wealthy brewery owner whose private collecting passion began when, aged 13, he bought two Solomon Island clubs. In 1914 he was elected to the Royal Anthropological Institute with which he maintained an association until 1937. He and his wife, Irene, established the Cranmore Ethnographic Museum in Chislehurst, Kent where they had moved in 1928, compiling the Cranmore Index of Pacific Material Culture based on James Edge-Partington's Index for the British Museum and forming a considerable library. Although the Beasleys collected artefacts worldwide – including Africa (particularly Benin), North-West America and Asia - their main focus was the Pacific. Objects were acquired from dealers, missionaries and from, or in exchanges with, various museums. Beasley's comprehensive monograph on Oceanic fish-hooks was published in 1928. The Cranmore Museum was damaged by bombing in World War II and in accordance with Beasley's will his widow, Irene M. Beasley offered the first selection of the collection (apart from a limited reservation for herself) as a donation to the British Museum. The gift of several thousand items became fully effective in 1944. Other named beneficiaries include the Pitt-Rivers Museum, Oxford; The Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, University of Cambridge; and National Museums, Scotland.

description_block:
A PAIR OF FAMILLE VERTE 'JIA SIDAO' VASES
19th century
Each of elongated ovoid shape surmounted by a waisted cylindrical neck and flaring mouth rim, decorated around the exterior with a continuous scene of ladies on horseback within a garden setting, above on a palatial terrace three scholar officials gaze at the horse riders admiringly, the necks decorated with boys at play. 
Each 40.4cm (15 7/8in) high. (2).

十九世紀 五彩月下跑馬圖瓶一對

The presence of horse-riding women usually identifies this subject matter as the story of 'The Female Troops of the Yang Family'. However, the crucial difference between this subject and that of the last Southern Song dynasty minister Jia Sidao, is the excited male figure on the balcony holding a fan. In the present lot, Jia Sidao is comically enjoying the pleasures of women riders at his Geling mansion by West Lake. His over-excitement leads him to almost step off the balcony.

According to the 'History of the Song Dynasty', emperor Duzong ascended the throne with the support of Jia Sidao (1213-1275) in 1264 after emperor Lizong passed away. He bestowed upon Jia the title of Imperial Teacher and a mansion at Geling in West Lake. Jia was allowed to attend the Imperial audience every three days and handle state affairs in his residence. At that time, all candidates who passed the Civil Examination were Jia's students and visited his mansion to deliver their gratitude. Jia wielded great influence throughout the government.

In 1269, Jia became more arrogant and requested retirement quoting health reasons. Emperor Duzong, in tears, tried to retain him. In the end, emperor Duzong gave in, exempting Jia from performing the ritual bow when greeting the throne and allowing him to attend the Imperial audience every ten days. A contemporary poem made a sarcastic remark of the situation that there is no prime minister at the court but in West Lake instead. When the Mongols besieged Xiangyang, Jia paid no attention but surrounded himself with beautiful concubines ranging from Palace ladies and prostitutes to nuns in his Geling mansion. Jia was eventually assassinated and considered an 'evil' minister that led to the ultimate conquest by the Mongols.

See a blue and white rouleau vase decorated with Jia Sidao holding a fan, Kangxi, illustrated in Folklore in Ming and Qing Porcelain, Hong Kong, 2019, pp.83-87.

Provenance: Dr Walter Rieder (1890-1986)

Dr Walter Rieder (1890-1986) served in the Swiss East Asia Mission (SOAM) in Qingdao, Shandong Province, between October 1930 and December 1951. The mission specialised in educational, literary and philanthropic work and Dr Rieder was in fact, not a theologian or missionary, but a teacher of mathematics, physics and science to high school students attached to the SOAM. His guiding principles were 'Creating understanding between different cultures' and 'Building bridges between East and West'. While in Qingdao, Dr Rieder collected a wide variety of Chinese art. The objects in the collection thus offer a unique window into the type of antiques that were on the market in Qingdao in the second quarter of the 20th century. As well as demonstrating his passion for Chinese art, his collection also reveals the personal friendships Dr Rieder forged with local artists, some of whom he knew from his teaching activities. Dr Rieder had a scholarly approach to studying his collection. Alongside many of his objects, meticulous notes can sometimes be found detailing his art historical commentaries. The collection was hence Dr Rieder's gateway to the history and culture of China. Objects from the collection were exhibited at the Kunsthaus in Interlaken, Switzerland in 2006 and 2018.

Historically, it was used by emperors for important ceremonies and banquets. The phrase "imperial use" (御用, yù yòng) indicates that this rug was specifically made for use within the Forbidden City, likely commissioned for the Imperial court during the Qing Dynasty.

〈一〉款識：雲水蕩晴空，孤颿萬里征。中原好景緻，江山一派青。时維甲子夏月，立中賢契属，二提劉津。碣石山樵。
鈐印：「二提」「碣石山樵」「水月」「銕肩」「才國楹印」「子孫永寶」「息心盦主」
〈二〉款識：澷道歸途山路險，家鄉即在白雲中。時在丁丑䆋七月，碣石山樵。
鈐印：「翰墨緣」「仌雪爲心」「子孫永寶」
〈三〉款識：雲山蒼蒼，雨氣茫茫。詩思佳處，溪橋之傍。峕維甲子夏，摹襄陽法於長春飬正書屋。碣石山樵劉準。二提
鈐印：「昌黎劉準」「平等」「銕肩」「才國楹印」
〈四〉款識：雲山雨霽，別具一番蒼潤之色，此中境界，非操觚三十年後恐未易到。丁丑秋七月，劉二提識。二提
鈐印：「易亭之印」「慎言」「才國楹印」
〈五〉款識：四面寰山，泉流不斷，僲境無人，雲橫白練。歲次丁丑秋七月。二提劉準寫。/蘆江寥濶，一望無際。飛蓬萬里，豁人胸臆。丁丑秋七月寫於養正書屋，劉二提。
鈐印：「仁山」「人品高師灋古」「碣石山樵」「立中」
〈六〉款識：昔人畫山水多用重色，黄子久晚年一變其法，獨用淡赭色，别具一種糁澹閒雅之概。然非磅礴之氣貫於其中，未足以盡其妙也。故後世宗之者恒有望塵莫及之慨。茲試略仿其意，未識能有合否？峕維丁丑秋七月，寫於長春養正書屋二提劉準并題。
鈐印：「二提」「準」「碣石山樵」「曾經滄海」「銕肩」
〈七〉款識：昨夜雨初晴，朝來烟如織。杖履訪幽棲，何惜衣衫濕。時維丁丑䆋七月寫於養正書屋，昌黎劉準。
鈐印：「二提」「準」「知白守黑」「息心盦主」
〈八〉款識：方壺圜嶠，神僲所居。徒聞其說，未見真蹟。兹覩斯圖，不禁油然相憶。丁丑秋七月，劉二提寫。
鈐印：「仌雪爲心」「碣石山樵」「立中書畫」

Peaches and bats are both highly auspicious motifs. Peaches symbolise longevity and Immortality, associated with the legendary peaches of immortality of Xi Wangmu, while bats represent blessings and good fortune because the word for bat (fu 蝠) is a homophone of fu (福), meaning happiness or good fortune. When combined, the motifs convey wishes for long life and abundant blessings. 

See a related yellow and russet jade carving of a 'bat and peach' 18th century, which was sold at Christie's New York, 21st March 2025, lot 897.

His brother Lt. Col. Sir Philip Lee Brocklehurst Bt, (1887-1975), Swythamley Park, near Macclesfield until 1975
Thence by descent

Both brothers were extensive travellers and explorers, Sir Philip having been on Shackleton's 1907 – 1909 Nimrod expedition to the Antarctic and who later travelled through both the Middle and Far East. His brother Courtney, who went with him to the Arctic in 1912 and later became game warden of the Sudan in the 1920s, then went on to travel extensively in China, Japan and Tibet in the 1930s, bringing back the first giant panda from Tibet to the UK.

Many of the artefacts collected on these travels were put on loan at the West Park Museum, which had been built by the Brocklehurst family for safe keeping during the war, and when he was killed in 1942 fighting with the Chindits in Burma, his brother Philip inherited the contents of the museum where they remained until after his death in 1975.
